earlier_scan.source_named: Lee, Ernest W. 1998. The contribution of Cat Gia Roglai to Chamic (Glottolog doctype: comparative, phonology); SEAlang archive unreachable (cert expired / timeouts).

new_statements.quote: p. 34: "It should be noted that the pretonic reflexes of voiced stops in CGR are without aspiration and the same is true in Haroi. Haroi does have an occasional allophonic aspiration of voiceless stops in pretonic position, but is unrelated to the source of the stop (Mundhenk and Goschnick 1977:5ff.). It would also be parallel to Utsat, which has voiceless aspirated stops reflecting original voiced stops in the tonic syllable (e.g. Maddieson and Pang 1993)." p. 47: "To my knowledge only ECham and CGR share the shift of PC *s- to tʰ- and that only in the tonic syllable."
new_statements.citation: Lee, Ernest W. 1998. The contribution of Cat Gia Roglai to Chamic. In David Thomas (ed.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 15: Further Chamic Studies (Pacific Linguistics A-89), 31-54. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A89.31
new_statements.locator: p. 34 (§2.2, PDF page 40) and p. 47 (§6.2, PDF page 53)
new_statements.rule_in_words: IMPLICIT ONLY. Lee never states where stress falls; he labels the presyllable of sesquisyllabic words the 'pretonic syllable' and the main (word-final) syllable the 'tonic syllable' (pp. 33, 34, 35, 47, 49), the standard Chamic/Mainland-SEA usage in which the final main syllable carries the stress and the presyllable is unstressed (with neutral vowel duration, p. 35). Read as: stress on the main = final syllable of the word; presyllables unstressed. The explicit family-level statement is Thurgood 1998 in the same volume, p. 61 (Proto-Chamic iambic: unstressed initial syllable + stressed main syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress discussion at all. Lee notes (p. 33) that CGR appears to be developing a Cham-type register system from initial voiced stops, and that the pretonic syllable has neutral vowel duration (p. 35).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, sesquisyllabic (presyllable + main syllable) words in elicited citation forms; data from about two hours of elicitation in 1974, which Lee calls 'very sketchy and some of it not completely reliable phonetically' (p. 31). 'Tonic' here is the SEA-linguistics term for the stressed main syllable, not a claim of lexical tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Lee 1998 describes the speech of two hamlets, Ap Cat Gia and Ap Binh Nghia-Cham (Xa Cat Rai, north of Phan Rang, Ninh Thuan), recorded in 1974; speakers call themselves Radlai. Lee explicitly does not treat it as a Southern Roglai dialect (sout3010) and contrasts it throughout with Northern Roglai (nort2994); it shares the Roglai final-nasal denasalisation but is otherwise Cham-like (register, *s- > th-). Glottolog cacg1235 = ISO roc = the 'Cac Gia' dialect of Cobbey 1977's four-way Raglai split. Data quality caveat from the author himself: ~2 hours of elicitation, 'very sketchy'.

sources.note: Whole paper is historical phonology of CGR (voiced stops/register, vowel length, nasalisation, *s- > th-, *r/*n > y/w, final *-p) from ~2 hours of 1974 fieldwork; no stress/accent section and no explicit statement of stress placement, but the presyllable is called the 'pretonic syllable' and the main (final) syllable the 'tonic syllable' throughout (pp. 33, 34, 35, 47, 49), i.e. main-syllable stress is assumed, not described.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham. 1998. Austronesian and Mon-Khmer components in the Proto Chamic vowel system. In David Thomas (ed.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 15: Further Chamic Studies (Pacific Linguistics A-89), 61-90. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A89.61
sources.note: p. 61 (family level, Proto-Chamic, not CGR-specific): 'this pre-Chamic Austronesian (An) language adopted the main-syllable stress of the neighbouring MK languages... the formerly disyllabic morphemes came to have an unstressed initial syllable followed by a stressed main syllable. This iambic PC stress pattern is certainly reflected in the contrasts between the vowel inventories of the pre-syllable and the main syllable.'
